rendering.title: 01 Rendering and Lifecycle
rendering.theory:
What is Rendering?

Rendering is the process of displaying a component's template in the browser. Angular updates the view when application data changes, using change detection to keep the UI in sync with the component's state.

What is the Component Lifecycle?

Every Angular component goes through different stages, from being created and initialized to being updated and eventually destroyed. Angular provides lifecycle hooks that allow us to execute code at specific stages of a component's existence.

Lifecycle Hooks

  1. constructor: Runs when the component is created. Not an Angular lifecycle hook.
  2. ngOnChanges: Runs when component inputs change.
  3. ngOnInit: Runs once when the component initializes.
  4. ngDoCheck: Runs during change detection.
  5. ngAfterContentInit: Runs once after projected content initializes.
  6. ngAfterContentChecked: Runs when projected content is checked.
  7. ngAfterViewInit: Runs once after the component view initializes.
  8. ngAfterViewChecked: Runs when the component view is checked.
  9. ngOnDestroy: Runs before the component is destroyed.

Component Visibility and Destruction

Angular provides different ways to control whether a component is visible or exists in the DOM. The important difference is whether the component is destroyed or simply hidden.

  • @if: Creates or destroys a component based on a condition. Its local state resets when recreated.
  • [hidden]: Hides an element without destroying its component. Its state is preserved.
  • display: none: Hides an element using CSS without removing it from the DOM. Its component state is preserved.

signals.title: 02 Signals
signals.theory:
What are Signals?

Signals are Angular's reactive state management system. They allow components to store values and automatically notify Angular when those values change, making it easier to keep the UI synchronized with application state.

Instead of manually tracking changes, Angular can track where signals are used and update the relevant parts of the application when their values change.

Types of Signals

  • signal(): Creates a writable reactive value that can be read and updated.
  • computed(): Creates a read-only value derived from other signals. It automatically recalculates when its dependencies change.
  • effect(): Runs side-effect logic when the signals it reads change. Useful for logging, synchronization, and interacting with external APIs.

rxjs-search.title: 03 RxJS Search
rxjs-search.theory:
What is RxJS?

RxJS (Reactive Extensions for JavaScript) is a library for working with asynchronous data and events over time. Angular uses RxJS extensively, especially for HTTP requests, forms, and event handling.

RxJS helps us manage multiple events, transform data, handle errors, and cancel outdated operations using Observables and operators.

What are Observables?

An Observable represents a stream of values that can arrive over time. Unlike a Promise, which resolves once, an Observable can emit multiple values. We subscribe to an Observable to react to its emissions.

Important RxJS Operators

  • combineLatest: Combines multiple Observables and emits their latest values whenever one changes, after each has emitted at least once.
  • startWith(): Provides an initial value so a stream can emit immediately.
  • debounceTime(300): Waits 300 milliseconds after the latest emission before emitting a value. Useful for search inputs.
  • distinctUntilChanged(): Prevents consecutive duplicate values from triggering unnecessary operations. A custom comparator can compare objects by their properties.
  • switchMap(): Switches to a new inner Observable and unsubscribes from the previous one. Useful for search requests where only the latest result matters.
  • catchError(): Handles errors and allows us to provide fallback values without breaking the entire search stream when placed inside switchMap.

Why Use RxJS for Search?

When a user types into a search field, each keystroke produces an event. Without RxJS, we might send unnecessary requests or display outdated results. By combining debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, and switchMap, we can wait until the user pauses typing, avoid duplicate searches, and cancel previous requests when a new search begins.

RxJS and HTTP Requests

Angular's HttpClient returns Observables. These allow us to transform responses, handle errors, and unsubscribe from requests that are no longer needed. In this exercise, we load a local people.json file through HttpClient and filter the results in the browser. This demonstrates reactive search behavior without requiring a real backend.

interop.title: 04 Signals and Observables / Interop
interop.theory:
What are Signals and Observables?

Signals and Observables are two ways to manage reactive data in Angular. Signals are designed for managing reactive state and updating the UI, while Observables are designed for handling streams of values over time, such as HTTP requests, user events, and timers.

What is a BehaviorSubject?

A BehaviorSubject is a special type of RxJS Subject that stores the latest value and immediately emits it to new subscribers. It requires an initial value and allows us to update its state using next().

Unlike a regular Observable, a BehaviorSubject can both emit values and be subscribed to. It is commonly used for sharing reactive state between components and services.

BehaviorSubject vs Signal

  • BehaviorSubject: Stores a current value and emits updates to subscribers. Values are updated using next() and can be read using getValue() or the value property.
  • signal(): Creates a reactive value managed by Angular. Values are read by calling the signal as a function and updated using set() or update().
  • AsyncPipe: Subscribes to an Observable in the template, displays its latest emitted value, and automatically unsubscribes when the view is destroyed.

What is RxJS Interop?

RxJS Interop allows Angular Signals and RxJS Observables to work together. Angular provides utilities in @angular/core/rxjs-interop to convert between these two reactive systems.

toSignal()

toSignal() converts an Observable into an Angular Signal. It subscribes to the Observable and updates the Signal whenever a new value is emitted. This allows Observable data to be accessed in templates using the Signal syntax.

Because Observables may not emit immediately, toSignal() can accept an initialValue. By default, the subscription is automatically cleaned up when the creating component or service is destroyed.

toObservable()

toObservable() converts an Angular Signal into an RxJS Observable. It tracks changes to the Signal and emits its latest stabilized value to subscribers.

This is useful when Signal-based state needs to be processed using RxJS operators such as debounceTime(), distinctUntilChanged(), or switchMap(). Multiple synchronous Signal updates may be combined into a single Observable emission.

When Should We Use Each?

  • Signals: Best suited for local component state, counters, UI visibility, and computed values.
  • Observables: Useful for asynchronous streams, HTTP requests, form changes, timers, and complex event processing.
  • BehaviorSubject: Useful when state needs to be shared with RxJS subscribers and the latest value must be immediately available.
  • toSignal(): Useful when displaying Observable data as Signal-based state in Angular components.
  • toObservable(): Useful when applying RxJS operators to Signal changes.

Why Is Interop Important?

Modern Angular applications often use Signals for managing UI state and RxJS for asynchronous operations. Interop utilities allow developers to combine both approaches without manually managing subscriptions or synchronizing values. This makes applications easier to organize, maintain, and extend.

testing.title: 05 Jest Testing
testing.theory:
What is Testing?

Testing is the process of verifying that our application behaves as expected. Instead of manually checking every feature after making changes, we write automated tests that execute our code and compare the actual results with expected results.

What is Jest?

Jest is a JavaScript testing framework used to write and run automated tests. In Angular, we can use Jest together with jest-preset-angular to test components, services, forms, and asynchronous behavior. Tests run in the terminal and are usually stored in .spec.ts files beside the code they test.

Types of Tests

  • Unit tests: Test a small piece of functionality, such as a method, component, or service, in isolation.
  • Integration tests: Verify that multiple parts work correctly together, such as a component interacting with a service.
  • End-to-end (E2E) tests: Simulate real user journeys through the application, such as logging in or submitting a form.

Important Testing Concepts

  • describe(): Groups related tests into a test suite.
  • it(): Defines an individual test case.
  • expect(): Checks whether an actual value matches the expected result.
  • TestBed: Angular's testing utility for configuring dependencies and creating components or services in a test environment.
  • jest.fn(): Creates a mock function that can track calls and return controlled values.
  • jest.spyOn(): Observes or replaces an existing object's method to verify how it is called.
  • jest.useFakeTimers(): Replaces real timers with controlled timers so we can test delays without waiting.
  • HttpTestingController: Allows us to inspect HTTP requests and simulate successful or failed responses without calling a real server.

What is Mocking?

Mocking means replacing a real dependency with a controlled version during testing. For example, instead of calling a real API, we can return predefined data. This makes tests faster, more predictable, and independent of external services.

What is the Test Pyramid?

The test pyramid describes a testing strategy with many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of end-to-end tests. Unit tests check individual behaviors quickly, while end-to-end tests verify that important user journeys work together.

Why Do We Write Tests?

Tests help us detect bugs, verify requirements, and safely change existing code. A good test checks observable behavior rather than implementation details. If we intentionally break a feature, its corresponding test should fail.

communication.title: 06 Inputs and Outputs
communication.theory:
What is Component Communication?

Angular applications are built using components that often need to exchange information. For example, a parent component might pass a username to a child, while the child notifies the parent when a button is clicked. Angular provides inputs and outputs to handle this communication.

How Does Data Flow?

Angular follows a one-way data flow model for component inputs. Data flows from parent to child through inputs, while events flow from child to parent through outputs. The parent owns the data it passes, and the child communicates changes by emitting events rather than directly modifying the parent's state.

Modern Input and Output APIs

  • input(): Declares an optional input with a default value or an input whose value may be undefined. The value is exposed as a read-only InputSignal.
  • input.required(): Declares a required input that the parent must provide. Angular checks this requirement during template compilation.
  • output(): Declares an output that allows a child component to emit values to its parent using emit().

Legacy Input and Output APIs

  • @Input(): Declares a property that receives data from a parent component.
  • @Output(): Declares an event that the parent can listen to.
  • EventEmitter: Emits values through an @Output property using emit().

Modern vs Legacy APIs

Both approaches solve the same parent-child communication problem. The modern APIs use input signals and output emitters, while the legacy APIs use decorators and EventEmitter. Signal inputs integrate naturally with computed() and Angular's reactive state system. The legacy APIs remain supported and are common in existing Angular applications.

When Should We Use Inputs and Outputs?

Use inputs when a parent needs to configure a child or provide data for display. Use outputs when a child needs to notify its parent about an action, such as a button click, selection, or form submission. This keeps components reusable and avoids unnecessary dependencies between them.

communication-patterns.title: 07 Other Communication Patterns
communication-patterns.theory:
What are Component Communication Patterns?

Angular provides different ways for components to exchange data and interact with each other. While inputs and outputs are commonly used for parent-child communication, other patterns are useful when components need to synchronize values, share state, or access child methods directly.

Two-Way Binding with model()

The model() API creates a writable Signal that supports two-way binding between parent and child. Unlike input(), which is read-only inside the child, model() allows both components to update the value. Angular automatically synchronizes changes using the [(property)] syntax.

Shared State with a Signal Service

A service can store a Signal that multiple components read and update. When sibling components inject the same service instance, they share the same reactive state. Updating the Signal in one component automatically updates the other. The service's provider scope determines how widely that state is shared.

Accessing a Child with viewChild()

The viewChild() API allows a parent component to access a child component or DOM element from its template. It returns a Signal containing the matching instance, or undefined when the child is absent. This is useful when the parent needs to call a public child method, such as focusing an input.

When Should We Use Each Pattern?

  • model(): Use for two-way binding when both parent and child need to update the same value, such as a checkbox or toggle.
  • Signal service: Use when multiple components need access to shared state, especially sibling components.
  • viewChild(): Use for imperative actions on a child, such as focusing an input, opening a dialog, or triggering a method.
